source: AI-assisted content generation (ChatGPT), synthesized from Cambodia MAFF/FIA Law on Animal Health and Production, FAOLEX Cambodia National Policy to Combat AMR, FAO Cambodia antimicrobial-use reporting
text: Responsible use of veterinary medicines matters because medicines protect animal health when used correctly, but inappropriate treatment can cause treatment failure, drug residues in meat/milk/eggs, and antimicrobial resistance. Cambodia's Law on Animal Health and Production regulates veterinary medicines, requires Khmer-language labels, and gives MAFF responsibility for technical standards; Cambodia has also adopted a national policy addressing antimicrobial resistance. Medicine should not be the first response to every sick animal — first observe carefully, consider disease, parasites, injury, nutrition, heat stress, or poor housing as possible causes, and involve a veterinarian or animal-health worker when treatment is needed. FAO's recent Cambodia work identifies incorrect antibiotic use among smallholders as an important AMR concern. The chatbot must never invent a medicine dose, injection volume, dilution, treatment duration, or withdrawal period, or substitute one product for another — these must come from a veterinarian, qualified animal-health professional, or the current registered product label for the specific animal, disease, formulation, and jurisdiction. A withdrawal period (time before meat/milk/eggs can safely enter the food supply) is product-specific and can never be inferred from the disease name or active ingredient alone. Vaccines and some medicines require controlled storage/cold-chain conditions that a smallholder may not have — coordinate with a veterinarian or animal-health worker rather than assuming home storage is adequate. Never mix, substitute, or double a dose because treatment isn't working — reassess with a professional instead. If several animals become sick at once, think beyond individual treatment (contagious disease, contaminated feed/water, poisoning, environmental change) and isolate/investigate rather than treating the whole group with an antibiotic by default. No specific local veterinary medicine, dose, withdrawal period, or price should be given for Preah Vihear without the exact registered product and current professional guidance.
